lesson.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
lesson.objective: Understand that in a right triangle the squares on the two legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse, and use it to find a missing side.

beats.sentence: Imagine a ladder leaning on a wall, and the ground, wall and ladder make a triangle.
The wall meets the ground at a perfect square corner, which we call a right angle.
The two sides touching that corner are called the legs, and we name them a and b.
The long slanted side across from the corner is the hypotenuse, and we call it c.
Notice the hypotenuse is always the longest side, because it faces the biggest angle.
Pythagoras found a surprisingly simple rule linking these three sides, and it only works with right angles.
Here is the trick: picture building a real square on each side of the triangle.
The square on leg a has area a squared, and the square on leg b has b squared.
The square on the hypotenuse is the biggest, with area c squared.
Amazingly, the two smaller squares together hold exactly as much area as the big one.
So we write the theorem as a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
This equation is the whole theorem, so keep it in mind as we try real numbers.
Say the ladder's foot is three metres from the wall and reaches four metres up.
Square each leg: three squared is nine, and four squared is sixteen.
Add them together and we get twenty five, which equals c squared.
Take the square root of twenty five, and the ladder must be five metres long.
So in any right triangle, the legs' squares add up to the hypotenuse squared.
Builders, navigators and game designers use this every day to measure distances they cannot reach directly.

suggestedQuestions: How do I find a leg if I know the hypotenuse?
Why does the theorem only work for right triangles?
What are Pythagorean triples like three, four, five?

recall.question: Which side of a right triangle is the hypotenuse?
options: The side opposite the right angle
Either side touching the right angle
recall.explanation: The hypotenuse faces the right angle and is always the longest side.

recall.question: What does a squared plus b squared equals c squared say about the squares on the sides?
options: The big square equals the two smaller squares combined
The small squares are each half the big one
recall.explanation: The areas of the squares on the two legs add up exactly to the area of the square on the hypotenuse.

recall.question: If the legs are three and four, how long is the hypotenuse?
recall.explanation: Nine plus sixteen is twenty five, and the square root of twenty five is five.
